anthropic/claude-opus-5-5.text:
**(1) First message to the user**

```text
gauntlet: question
One load-bearing premise is corrected, and the rest are unverified. Acceptance row 3 ("The export of a 10k-row report completes in under 60s") depends on a way to fetch a large report without loading it all at once. The gather draft records that paging is unimplemented, so that dependency is missing. The design continues with paging treated as new work. The draft records no evidence that the 60s target is impossible, so the row stays in-scope as written.

Two premises are unverified because I used no tools this turn. The first is that `src/export/csv.ts` builds its output from the table's column definitions. The second is that the reports page has no export action. The lookups are a read of `src/export/csv.ts` and a search of the reports page component for an export action. Both claims carry into `## Problem` as stated assumptions until those reads confirm them.

I am assuming the `### acme/mailer` row ("Exports are emailed to the requesting user.") is `elsewhere: acme/mailer`. The overrides `## Issue tracker` names this repo as `acme/widgets`, so that row belongs to the mailer repo and adds no work here.

The framing holds: I checked that the ask maps onto an existing serializer (`src/export/csv.ts`) instead of a new one, and that the table's column list is the source the export rows name. I also traced row 3's implicit dependency on paged data access and found it missing, as stated above. Neither check gave a cited case that the ticket is misdiagnosed or already solved.

Where should the Export CSV button appear on the reports page?
A) beside the report title
B) in a toolbar above the table
C) other - name it
Recommendation: A - the title area is page-level, and the export covers the whole report rather than one table control.
```

*(The user answers A, beside the report title. The next question asks which columns export, and the user answers: the visible table columns, in table order. That answer becomes the Design reading of row 2. Row 2 stays `in-scope` with its text unchanged.)*

**(2) Approaches message**

```text
gauntlet: question
First, a restatement of the missing dependency. Row 3 needs paged data access for a 10k-row report. The gather draft says paging is unimplemented. I would confirm this by searching the report data path for a page, offset, or cursor parameter. The recorded result is that none exists. Whether one unpaged fetch of 10k rows fits in 60s is not measured.

The approaches differ on how the 10k rows reach the serializer.

I recommend B: reuse the CSV serializer and add paging. The button sits beside the report title. It walks the report's rows page by page and passes each page through `src/export/csv.ts`, using the visible table columns in table order. This is the only option that gives row 3 a bounded data path instead of a hope that one large fetch is fast enough. It keeps one serializer and one column source. The cost is new paging in the report data path, which other callers of that path will also see. Paging needs its own test against a 10k-row fixture.
Removes: none
Adds: Export CSV button beside the report title; page/cursor parameter on the report data fetch; paged export loop that feeds `src/export/csv.ts`; test for the button and visible-column order; 10k-row timing test
Pattern: follows `src/export/csv.ts`, which serializes from the table's column definitions, and extends the shared report data path rather than adding a second one.

A, reuse-only, needs no new construct. The button calls `src/export/csv.ts` on the full report in one fetch. It is the smallest change and touches no shared data path. It meets rows 1 and 2. It cannot be shown to meet row 3, because the single fetch is unpaged and its 10k-row time is unmeasured. Without paging, row 3 has no lever if that fetch is too slow.
Removes: none
Adds: Export CSV button beside the report title; single-fetch call into `src/export/csv.ts`; button and column-order test; 10k-row timing test
Pattern: follows `src/export/csv.ts` unchanged.

C drops the assumption that export runs on the reports page. A server-side export generates the file and the button downloads it. This option solves row 3 where the data lives. However, it needs a new endpoint and probably a second serialization path, because `src/export/csv.ts` is the page-side serializer and nothing shows it runs server-side. That would split the column source in two.
Removes: none
Adds: server export endpoint; server-side CSV generation; download button beside the report title; endpoint test; 10k-row timing test
Pattern: cuts across `src/export/csv.ts` as the single serializer by adding a parallel path beside it.

What would flip my recommendation: if a 10k-row single fetch measures well under 60s, A wins, because paging would then be unneeded work.

Which approach should the design take?
A) reuse-only - single fetch through the existing serializer
B) reuse the serializer and add paging
C) server-side export endpoint
Recommendation: B - it is the only option with a bounded path for row 3 that still keeps one serializer and one column source.
```

github-copilot/gpt-6.1-sol.text:
### 1. First message to the user

gauntlet: question
The framing holds against the supplied observations: the reports page lacks an export action, and `src/export/csv.ts` already uses the table’s column definitions, supporting reuse rather than a second serializer. Primary-code traces of the reports loader, column visibility/order, and serializer callers remain unverified because only the gathered observations are available. Paging is unimplemented; that does not establish that exporting 10,000 rows within 60 seconds is impossible, so that acceptance criterion stays in scope. The email criterion belongs to the nonmember repository `acme/mailer` and is recorded as `elsewhere: acme/mailer`, not added to this implementation.

Where should the Export CSV button appear?
A) Beside the report title.
B) In the table’s action toolbar.
C) Other — name the location.
Recommendation: A - it makes the report-wide action visible without tying it to an individual table row.

### 2. Approaches message, after the recorded answers

I recommend **reusing the existing CSV serializer and adding paging**, as you selected. The button will sit beside the report title, and the export will contain the visible table columns in table order.

The supplied draft supports serializer reuse through `src/export/csv.ts` and identifies paging as missing. It does not establish whether the report data API already supports pagination: no API contract or loader trace is supplied. The visible-column projection and serializer callers are also unverified, and no timing measurement establishes compliance with the 10,000-row, under-60-second requirement. Those are implementation dependencies to verify, not reasons to weaken the requirement. Email delivery remains owned by `acme/mailer`.

The approaches differ in **where report traversal and CSV generation run**:

**A. Extend the existing reports-page export path with paging — recommended and selected.**  
Add the title-adjacent button, obtain the visible columns in their displayed order, retrieve all report pages, and pass their rows through the existing serializer. This is the minimal reuse-only candidate: extend existing constructs rather than introduce a separate export service or serializer. The serializer’s existing callers must be checked before changing any shared signature; ideally its implementation remains unchanged.

This has the smallest architectural footprint, but client memory, page-request latency, and available API pagination affect whether it meets the timing requirement. Paging alone is not proof of performance.

Removes: none.  
Adds: reports-page export action and state; paged row traversal; visible-column/order wiring; export behavior, failure, and performance tests.  
Pattern: follows the table-column reuse identified in `src/export/csv.ts`; avoids a parallel CSV contract.

**B. Generate the export on the server, reusing the serializer where compatible.**  
The same button requests a server-generated CSV. The server traverses report pages and returns the download. This drops the assumption that the browser must collect all rows and can reduce browser memory pressure, but introduces an endpoint, server-side authorization and report-query handling, and download-error behavior. Compatibility of the existing serializer with that runtime is unverified.

Removes: none.  
Adds: export endpoint; server-side report traversal and CSV response handling; reports-page download integration; endpoint, authorization, column-order, and performance tests.  
Pattern: preserves the column-definition contract identified in `src/export/csv.ts` only if that contract can be shared; duplicating its column logic would create drift.

I would keep A unless verified API constraints or representative measurements show that client-side traversal cannot meet the retained performance requirement; that evidence would favor B.
